title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles

epigraph.quote: Every enduring software franchise begins by solving a messy, paper-bound bottleneck that larger vendors ignore—yet scaling from a niche toolmaker into a multi-product platform tests capital discipline far more than code.
epigraph.author: Institutional Field Notes

web_blocks.html: Vijay Gupta founded SoftTech Engineers Limited in Pune in June 1996 [1][18]. He is an M.Tech alumnus of IIT Bombay (1986) who previously worked at Crompton Greaves and Godrej & Boyce [18]. His first commercial product, STRUDS (Structural Design and Detailing Software), served Indian civil and structural engineers [18]. It helped them comply with Indian Standard (IS) building codes [18]. STRUDS built SoftTech's reputation across domestic design consultancies for fifteen years [18]. In 2011, the company sold the STRUDS intellectual property to UK-based CSC [18]. That sale marked SoftTech's first big pivot: leaving desktop structural tools to focus on municipal e-governance and automated plan scrutiny.

The second act began in 2005 with the launch of AutoDCR (Automated Development Control Regulations) [18]. Indian urban local bodies faced major delays checking architectural CAD drawings by hand [16][17]. Engineers had to verify complex municipal bye-laws, floor-space-index (FSI) rules, and setback norms [16][17]. AutoDCR automated this geometry check against encoded local rules, cutting subjectivity and approval times [16]. Early wins at Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) and Greater Mumbai (MCGM) gave SoftTech a strong GovTech foothold [16][17]. Over the next decade, the firm added PWIMS for state public works departments and Opticon ERP for private contractors [3][4].

web_blocks.caption: Corporate Evolution & Capital Milestones (1996–2026)
rows: Founded in Pune by Vijay Gupta (IIT Bombay); entered structural CAD software [1][18].
Pioneered automated CAD building-plan scrutiny for Indian municipal corporations [18].
Monetized legacy desktop tool to fund GovTech and municipal e-governance expansion [18].
Raised ~₹22.81 Cr at ₹78–80/share to fund product development and working capital [11].
Wholly-owned Finnish subsidiary created to build AI/ML-enabled BIM products for global markets [12].
German construction-tech leader RIB Software invested strategically for global permit automation [13].
Migrated from NSE Emerge SME platform to NSE Main Board and BSE on Feb 25, 2022 [10].
Issued warrants/equity to Florintree Technologies and Einstein Work Pte. Ltd.; promoter stake fell to 18.89% [1][14].
Acquired Envee IT (MIDC digital solutions) and unified products under the cloud-native CIVIT suite [4][15].
web_blocks.takeaway: SoftTech repeatedly pivoted from desktop engineering tools to GovTech projects, and now to cloud/BIM platforms, funded heavily by external equity dilution rather than internal free cash flow.

web_blocks.html: SoftTech's public-market journey began in May 2018 with an SME IPO on NSE Emerge [11]. The issue raised about ₹22.81 Cr at ₹78–₹80 per share [11]. Two months later, in July 2018, management formed SoftTech Finland Oy to lead global Building Information Modeling (BIM) and AI/ML work [12]. In 2020, Germany's RIB Software SE (later acquired by Schneider Electric) took a strategic stake in SoftTech [13]. The two firms partnered on global building-permit automation [13]. On February 25, 2022, SoftTech migrated from the SME platform to the Main Board of the NSE and BSE [10].

Operationally, the post-IPO decade shows three clear business cycles rather than smooth compounding [1]. First, from FY19 to FY21, revenue fell from ₹63 Cr to ₹58 Cr in FY20 and ₹42 Cr in FY21 [1]. COVID-19 lockdowns halted municipal tenders and slowed government payments, pushing debtor days from 109 in FY19 to 293 in FY21 [1]. Second, from FY22 to FY24, revenue recovered from ₹57 Cr to ₹79 Cr [1]. Yet net profit stayed flat at ₹3 Cr to ₹5 Cr as depreciation jumped from ₹4 Cr (FY19) to ₹13 Cr (FY24) [1]. That surge happened as capitalized software hit the P&L [1]. Third, from FY25 to FY26, revenue jumped from ₹95.25 Cr to ₹132.90 Cr (+39.5% YoY) [1][2]. Even so, consolidated net profit stayed thin at ₹5.33 Cr (4.0% margin) [2]. Rising depreciation (₹22.83 Cr) and doubtful-debt provisions (₹12.08 Cr) absorbed most of the operating gain [2].

web_blocks.title: The Dilution & Ownership Arc
paragraphs: A defining trait of SoftTech's history is the steady drop in promoter ownership. After the May 2018 IPO, the firm issued preferential convertible warrants and equity [1][2]. Key allotments went to Florintree Technologies LLP (2022) and Einstein Work Pte. Ltd. (late 2024) [1][14]. As a result, total equity capital grew from ₹9 Cr in FY19 to ₹13.84 Cr in FY26 [1][2].

Over the three years through H1 FY27, promoter shareholding fell by 21.6 percentage points to 18.89%, down from 32.05% in March 2024. Meanwhile, public shareholding rose to 81.12% and FII ownership fell to 0.00% [1]. For a founder-led software firm, sub-20% promoter skin-in-the-game is a key governance risk.

web_blocks.html: Capital raises also reshaped the share register in ways that matter to minority buyers [1][14]. In late 2022, Florintree Technologies LLP (led by Mathew Cyriac) invested ₹25 Cr via convertible warrants [14]. That stake crossed 15% before Florintree trimmed and exited blocks in 2025–2026 [14]. In late 2024 and early 2025, SoftTech held an Extraordinary General Meeting for another preferential issue [9]. Singapore-based Einstein Work Pte. Ltd. took a ~19.5% post-issue stake alongside smaller strategic allotments [1][9]. Those infusions lifted cash and bank balances to ₹32.91 Cr at March 31, 2026 [2]. They also funded the August 2024 purchase of Envee Information Technology Pvt. Ltd., a MIDC digital workflow specialist [15]. However, the raises expanded equity capital from ₹9 Cr to ₹13.84 Cr and diluted promoter holding to 18.89% [1][2].

web_blocks.mechanism: Expanded from domestic niche software into global aviation, logistics, and HR cloud suites by capitalizing heavy R&D onto the balance sheet while chasing multi-year enterprise/government implementations.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Revenue scaled past ₹500 Cr, yet capitalized intangibles, elongated receivable cycles, and rising amortization kept ROE depressed and forced repeated equity raises.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Top-line acceleration in Indian vertical software often masks cash-flow strain if R&D capitalization and long-dated receivables outpace operating profit.

book_paragraphs: When you and I sit down to study a twenty-eight-year-old software company from Pune, the first thing we have to separate is longevity from compounding. SoftTech Engineers has survived nearly three decades in one of the toughest corners of Indian enterprise technology: selling software to municipal corporations, state public works departments, and construction contractors.

Vijay Gupta, an IIT Bombay M.Tech graduate, started the company in 1996 with a structural design package called STRUDS. That was a classic desktop engineering tool, and he ran it for fifteen years before selling the product to CSC in the UK in 2011. Think about what that tells us about the founder: he knows how to build domain-specific engineering code that solves real local compliance problems, and he is willing to pivot when a product matures.

The pivot that defined modern SoftTech happened in 2005 with AutoDCR. If you have ever watched a builder or architect try to get a building plan approved in an Indian city, you know the nightmare: thick paper rolls, subjective interpretations of Development Control Rules, and months of waiting. AutoDCR read the CAD drawing automatically and checked it against local building bye-laws. Winning Pune Municipal Corporation and Greater Mumbai gave SoftTech a genuine crown jewel.

Yet as you and I trace the arc from the 2018 SME IPO through the 2022 mainboard migration to FY26, a second pattern emerges alongside the product story. SoftTech did not fund its expansion into Finland, Germany, Dubai, and the cloud-native CIVIT suite out of surplus free cash flow. Instead, it funded it through a steady stream of borrowings and preferential equity issuances, diluting the promoter stake all the way down to 18.89%.

Let's trace the capital raises in detail, because this is where most retail investors lose the thread. In late 2022, SoftTech brought in Florintree Technologies through a ₹25 Cr convertible warrant issue, pushing Florintree's stake past 15%. Then in late 2024, the company went back to the well again, approving a major preferential allotment to Einstein Work Pte. Ltd. in Singapore and buying Envee Information Technology for MIDC digital workflows.

Think about what happens to a founder's alignment through that sequence. Every time you issue preferential shares or warrants to fund R&D, overseas subsidiaries, and working capital, the pie gets sliced thinner. By 2025–2026, Florintree had pared down its stake via block sales, FII ownership sat at zero, and Vijay Gupta's promoter group held just 18.89% of the company, down 21.6 percentage points in three years.

That does not mean the business is fraudulent or empty. It means the business has historically been a net consumer of outside equity rather than a self-funding cash machine. You and I need to keep that distinction front and center as we examine the products in Chapter 2.

Step back with me to 1996 in Pune, long before 'GovTech' or 'Digital Twin' existed in any Indian investor presentation. Vijay Gupta, an IIT Bombay M.Tech graduate, started SoftTech Engineers with a very practical engineering problem: structural engineers and municipal town planners in India were still checking building blueprints by hand, ruler, and red ink. SoftTech's first commercial success, STRUDS, tackled structural design and analysis, and selling STRUDS to Computer Sciences Corporation (CSC) of the UK in 2011 gave the company both validation and early capital to double down on its next big bet: AutoDCR.

If you want to understand why SoftTech survived for nearly three decades while hundreds of small Pune IT shops vanished, look at that 2005–2015 AutoDCR wave. Once a major city like Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) or the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM) embedded AutoDCR into its building-approval workflow, switching it out became an administrative nightmare. Architects, structural engineers, and municipal clerks all learned the same CAD layer conventions. By the time SoftTech listed on the NSE Emerge SME platform in May 2018, raising ₹22.81 Cr at ₹78–₹80 per share. And later migrated to the Main Board in February 2022, it looked like a classic sticky vertical-software franchise.

Yet every corporate pivot leaves footprints on the balance sheet. Between 2018 and 2026, SoftTech didn't stay a simple Indian municipal software vendor. It incorporated SoftTech Finland Oy in 2018 to chase AI/ML-enabled BIM in Europe, took a strategic investment from Germany's RIB Software SE in 2020, rebranded its suite under the CIVIT cloud umbrella, and acquired Envee Information Technology in 2024. Each move expanded the addressable market on paper, but each move also pulled more engineering hours into capitalized intangibles and stretched the gap between accounting revenue and collected cash.

book_callouts.title: Why Survival Is Not the Same as Capital Efficiency
book_callouts.text: Ask yourself as we read the next five chapters: when a software company grows revenue from ₹42 Cr in FY21 to ₹133 Cr in FY26, why did net profit barely budge from ₹3 Cr to ₹5 Cr, and why did the founder's stake shrink below 19%? The answer lies in the gap between accounting revenue and cash conversion.

book_subsections.title: Three Business Cycles in Eight Years
paragraphs: Look at the rhythm of SoftTech's revenue since FY19. In FY19, the company posted ₹63 Cr of sales and ₹7 Cr of net profit, an 11% net margin that looked like a healthy niche software business. Then came FY20 and the pandemic. Municipal offices shut down, tender decisions froze, and sales fell to ₹42 Cr in FY21 while debtor days stretched to an astonishing 293 days.

Between FY22 and FY24, revenue climbed back from ₹57 Cr to ₹79 Cr, and then in FY25 and FY26 it surged to ₹95 Cr and ₹133 Cr. On a headline revenue chart, that looks like a classic breakout. But you and I never stop at the top line. While sales more than tripled from the FY21 trough, depreciation and amortization climbed from ₹4 Cr in FY19 to ₹22.83 Cr in FY26. Every rupee of operating profit gained by winning bigger contracts was largely absorbed by the amortization of previously capitalized software.

Meanwhile, the balance sheet expanded through subsidiaries in Finland, Singapore, the US, the UK, Germany, and Dubai, plus the acquisition of Envee Information Technology in August 2024. Yet in FY26, standalone PBT was ₹12.99 Cr while consolidated PBT was only ₹8.93 Cr, meaning the subsidiary network as a whole was still a net drag on profitability.

callouts.title: The Dilution Lesson
callouts.text: In a capital-light software compounder, the founder's stake rarely needs to drop from over 40% to 18.89% in a few years. Whenever you see heavy dilution alongside flat net profits, check whether new equity is funding growth or plugging working capital and R&D burn.

book_subsections.title: Why the Subsidiary Network Matters to the Origin Story
paragraphs: Between 2018 and 2025, SoftTech didn't just stay in Pune. It incorporated or acquired SoftTech Finland Oy, SoftTech Engineers Inc. in the US, SoftTech Government Solutions Inc., SoftTech Digital Pte. Ltd. in Singapore, SoftTech Digital Software LLC in Dubai, SoftTech Digital Solutions Limited in the UK, SoftTech Digital AG in Germany, AmpliNxt Private Limited (its AECO startup incubator), and Envee Information Technology.

On a corporate org chart, nine subsidiaries across four continents look impressive. In the audited FY26 accounts, however, the statutory auditors note that four of those subsidiaries are management-drawn and immaterial (generating ₹1.49 Cr revenue and losing ₹1.58 Cr). Meanwhile, the consolidated group earned ₹8.93 Cr PBT against the standalone Indian parent's ₹12.99 Cr PBT. Building a global footprint is easy to announce; making those overseas entities self-sustaining is the hard part.

callouts.title: Founder Grit vs. Capital Allocation
callouts.text: Ask yourself: would SoftTech's owners have been richer today if management had focused purely on dominating Indian municipal GovTech and distributing surplus cash, rather than funding eight global subsidiaries with diluted equity?

book_subsections.title: Why the 2018–2026 Pivot Matters for Today's Investor
paragraphs: Notice how SoftTech's revenue cycle mirrors India's urban infrastructure and municipal digitization waves. During COVID-19 in FY21, municipal tender activity froze and revenue contracted 28% from ₹58 Cr to ₹42 Cr. When urban construction roared back in FY22 through FY26, revenue compounded from ₹42 Cr to ₹133 Cr, a more than threefold expansion in five years. That recovery proved that municipal demand for automated plan scrutiny is real and durable.

At the same time, look at what happened to the shareholding register during that recovery. At the 2018 SME IPO, promoter holding stood near 40%. Over the last three years alone, promoter stake declined by 21.6 percentage points down to 18.89%. Meanwhile, institutional foreign ownership (FII) sits at 0.00%. Whenever a founder-led small-cap software company scales revenue 3x while the promoter group's ownership shrinks below 20%, you must ask whether the business is generating enough self-funded cash or relying on equity dilution and outside capital.
